content.title: About
content.content: Canned asparagus consists of cooked asparagus spears packed in a jar with added fat to enhance flavor and preserve texture. The product is ready to eat and is commonly used in salads, side dishes, and hot meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus has been cultivated since ancient Rome and is one of the first spring vegetables.
Canning allows the vegetable to retain its nutrients for up to three years when stored properly.
Adding fat (usually a vegetable oil) improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K.
Canned asparagus jars are often identified with the USDA code “4598”.
Heat processing enhances aromatic compounds that give asparagus its distinctive flavor.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Asparagus provides glutathione and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of canned asparagus contains about 25 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly choice.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned vegetables often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Allergy to added oil
items.content: If a specific vegetable oil is used, individuals with oil sensitivities may react.

items.title: Bacterial risk from compromised cans
items.content: Bulging or damaged cans can harbor harmful bacteria and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned asparagus can be eaten cold in salads, warmed in the microwave, or added to soups and stews. If desired, drain excess fat and drizzle with olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the contents to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3‑4 days.

cheese-cottage-creamed-large-or-small-cu.title: Creamed Cottage Cheese, Large or Small Curds

content.title: About
content.content: Creamed cottage cheese is a soft, mildly acidic dairy product made from skimmed or partially skimmed milk. It is available in large‑curd or small‑curd varieties, offering a creamy texture and a subtle, slightly sweet flavor. Cottage cheese is widely used as a base for desserts, fillings, and healthy meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese has been produced since ancient times, with early records from Egypt and the Middle East.
Large‑curd cottage cheese retains a distinct grainy texture, while small‑curd versions are smoother and ideal for baking.
In many cuisines it is a staple for dishes such as cheese pancakes, stuffed dumplings, and creamy salads.
Modern processing often enriches cottage cheese with vitamin B‑complex and calcium.
It is commonly served with fruit, honey, or fresh herbs as a light snack.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Cottage cheese provides complete whey and casein proteins that support muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium contributes to strong bones and teeth and plays a role in muscle contraction.

items.title: Low‑fat options
items.content: Reduced‑fat cottage cheese is suitable for calorie‑controlled diets while still delivering nutrients.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Traditionally cultured cottage cheese may contain live lactic‑acid bacteria that support gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose sensitivity may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming cottage cheese.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause skin reactions, swelling, or respiratory issues.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some cottage cheese varieties are salted; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Cottage cheese spoils quickly; discard it if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy cottage cheese on its own, blend it into smoothies, make cheese pancakes, stuff dumplings, or incorporate it into salads, dips, and desserts. It pairs well with berries, honey, nuts, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cottage cheese in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container. It typically stays fresh for 5‑7 days. For longer storage, it can be frozen, though the texture may become crumbly.

cheese-spread-american-or-cheddar-cheese.title: Cheese spread, American or Cheddar cheese base

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese spread is a smooth, creamy paste made from melted American or Cheddar cheese. It has a rich buttery flavor with a mild tang typical of Cheddar. The product is commonly used as a spread, dip, or ingredient in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: American cheese was created in the early 20th century to extend the shelf life of traditional cheeses.
Cheddar originated in England’s Cheddar region in the 12th century and is now one of the world’s most popular cheeses.
Cheese spreads often contain small amounts of emulsifiers and stabilizers to keep a uniform texture.
In the United States, American‑cheese‑based spreads are a staple in fast‑food burgers and sandwiches.
There are many flavor variations: herb‑infused, spicy, smoked, or blended with blue‑cheese crumbles.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese spread provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Protein from the cheese helps maintain muscle mass and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Phosphorus content
items.content: Phosphorus contributes to cellular function and energy production.

items.title: Potential probiotic cultures
items.content: Some fermented cheese spreads may contain beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese spreads are often salty, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: They contain saturated fats that may affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may react to cheese spread.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Commercial varieties may include preservatives and emulsifiers that can cause sensitivities in some consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread it on bread, crackers, or vegetable sticks, use as a burger topping, stir into sauces, casseroles, or potato dishes. It also pairs well with fruits, nuts, or as a dip for chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the spread refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Orange juice, 100%, frozen, not reconstituted is a completely natural juice obtained from fresh oranges and quickly frozen without any added water, sugar, or preservatives. The juice retains the full spectrum of vitamins, minerals, and aromatic compounds characteristic of fresh orange juice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flash freezing preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C, which degrades quickly in liquid juice.
The juice is made from sweet orange varieties that do not require additional sweetening.
IQF (Individually Quick Frozen) technology keeps the texture and flavor close to fresh juice.
Frozen juice can be stored at home for up to 12 months while remaining safe to drink.
Unlike concentrates, this juice does not need reconstitution, eliminating the risk of flavor alteration.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division, especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties that protect blood vessels.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup (250 ml) of frozen juice contains about 110 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges, such as itching, swelling, or hives.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although unsweetened, the juice naturally contains fructose; people with diabetes should account for its intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the juice in the refrigerator or at room temperature, then stir and enjoy as a refreshing drink. It can also be used in smoothies, cocktails, sauces, and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen juice at –18 °C in an airtight package. After thawing, consume within 2–3 days, store in the refrigerator, and do not refreeze.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-eaten-no-.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel eaten, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potato is a whole tuber cooked without added fat. The skin is left on, preserving most of the dietary fiber and micronutrients. Potato is a major source of carbohydrates, B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and potassium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century and quickly became a staple food.
The skin contains more fiber and antioxidants than the flesh.
Roasting at high temperature creates aromatic compounds that give the characteristic taste and aroma.
There are over 4 000 potato varieties differing in colour, shape, and starch content.
Potatoes can be stored in a cool, dark place for several months without quality loss.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained satiety and a steady blood‑glucose level.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C and antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, while skin antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The skin supplies fiber that promotes digestive health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B9 are involved in protein metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Green spots and sprouting can contain solanine, a toxin that should be removed.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Roasted potatoes have a high GI, so people with diabetes should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to potato may occur.

items.title: Foodborne illness from improper storage
items.content: Storing in warm conditions can cause spoilage and toxin formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potato can be served as a standalone dish, cut into wedges, added to salads, soups, or used as a side. The skin is edible, especially when well‑washed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh potatoes in a cool, dark, dry place at 4‑10 °C. Do not refrigerate raw potatoes as it can alter flavor. Roasted potatoes keep in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Salsa, pico de gallo is a fresh Mexican sauce made from finely diced tomatoes, onion, chili pepper, cilantro, lime juice, and salt. It has a bright, slightly spicy flavor and a crunchy texture, perfect as a dip or a topping for dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pico de gallo literally means “little rooster’s beak,” but in cooking it refers to finely chopped ingredients.
Traditionally the salsa is uncooked, preserving maximum vitamins and aromas.
There are many regional variations that differ by type of pepper and may include fruits like mango.
Salsa is commonly served with tortillas, tacos, guacamole, and used as a meat marinade.
In the United States salsa has become the most popular condiment in fast‑food restaurants, surpassing ketchup.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes and lime provide vitamin C, which supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Salsa is low in calories, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes has anti‑inflammatory properties and supports heart health.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Cilantro and lime add flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Capsaicin from chili peppers stimulates gastric juice production and aids digestion.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tomatoes, onion, or chili peppers.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Very hot salsa can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt intake may raise blood pressure; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: If left at room temperature too long, salsa can develop bacterial growth; follow storage guidelines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use salsa as a dip for chips, tortillas, or raw vegetables, add it to tacos, burritos, salads, marinate meat, or serve it with fish and seafood. Adjust the heat level by adding more or less chili to suit your taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store salsa in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions; after thawing, stir as the texture may change.
